summary: Explains how to handle multiple dialog usages in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). A single SIP dialog can carry several related associations, such as a call and a subscription, that have separate lifetimes but share state. The document describes the problems this causes and recommends how to process them correctly.

plainLanguage.summary: A SIP dialog can carry more than one related activity, such as a call and a subscription. Because the activities end independently but share state, this memo explains the handling problems and recommends avoiding new uses of this pattern.

subtitle: Why multiple SIP dialog usages are difficult to handle and how applications can avoid them.

tldr.problem: Several independent SIP associations can share one dialog, so they have separate lifetimes but also share dialog state.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes how usages begin and end, surveys the effects of failure responses, and explains how requests are matched to usages.
tldr.outcome: It argues that new applications should avoid requiring multiple usages and discusses alternatives for existing cases. The document makes no normative statements.

today: RFC 5057 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo explicitly makes no normative statements.

sections.title: Dialogs and Dialog Usages
sections.content:
A SIP method can create a dialog and an associated dialog usage. An INVITE creates an invite usage; SUBSCRIBE and REFER create subscription usages. A dialog may contain one invite usage and multiple subscription usages. REGISTER and PUBLISH do not create a dialog or usage.

Usages share dialog state such as Call-ID, tags, sequence numbers, route set, contacts, remote target, and secure flag. A subscription's duration is usage-specific. A dialog begins with its first usage and remains until its last usage ends, which means a failure or change can affect one usage or the whole dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: A dialog is a shared SIP relationship, and a usage is one activity within it. The activities can have separate lifetimes even though they share some state.

sections.title: Examples: Transfer and Subscriptions
sections.content:
In the transfer example, Alice and Bob first establish an invite usage. A REFER and the related NOTIFY exchange create a subscription usage within the same dialog. When that subscription ends, the invite usage remains until the call is ended.

In the reciprocal-subscription example, each participant subscribes to the other's presence within one dialog. The subscriptions have different expiration times. Ending one subscription does not end the other or remove the shared dialog state while another usage remains.
sections.plainLanguage: A call can remain active after a related subscription ends. Two subscriptions can also share a dialog while each keeps its own timer.

sections.title: Creating, Ending, and Matching Usages
sections.content:
The messages that create or destroy a usage depend on its type. Invite usages are associated with INVITE processing and can end through BYE or certain failure responses. Subscription usages arise from SUBSCRIBE, REFER, or NOTIFY processing and can end through termination, timeout, or expiration.

The memo classifies failure effects as transaction-only, usage-ending, or dialog-ending. It highlights the ambiguity of a 481 response and recommends treating it as ending the usage, unless it was the last one. Request matching depends on method and, for subscription messages, the Event header. The memo also discusses target refresh requests, timeouts, refusing new usages, and replacing usages.
sections.plainLanguage: When a SIP request fails, an implementation needs to know whether the request, one activity, or the whole dialog is affected. Different requests are matched to usages using their method and headers.

sections.title: Avoiding Multiple Usages
sections.content:
The memo says correct processing of multiple usages is not fully understood and is difficult to implement, which can lead to interoperability problems. It recommends that new applications not require endpoints to create multiple usages and that endpoints handle existing cases carefully.

The transfer example uses a REFER within an existing dialog for reasons related to reaching the intended endpoint, associating the transfer with the call, and authorization. The memo describes alternatives using a globally routable user-agent URI and dialog-identification mechanisms so a request can be sent outside the existing dialog while still referring to it.
sections.plainLanguage: New designs should avoid putting separate activities into one dialog. A request can instead start outside that dialog and carry information that identifies the related dialog.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says security risks depend on the particular application and implementation. Multiple usages add complexity to the state that endpoints track, and the security considerations of the underlying SIP specifications still apply.

Applications that use multiple usages need to account for peers that handle usage termination differently. Applications that refuse additional usages also need to consider that some peers may respond by ending the entire dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations must track which activity a request belongs to and what a failure ends. Different assumptions at the two endpoints can cause calls or subscriptions to stop unexpectedly.
